svg.title: Five long-context benchmarks and what each one finds
svg.desc: A hand-drawn table of five benchmarks. Needle-in-a-haystack hides one fact in a long context and asks for it back; frontier models score in the high nineties well past a hundred thousand tokens, so it barely degrades, and it is the result behind the "long context just works" pitch. RULER adds multi-needle retrieval, distractor keys, multi-value lookups, and variable tracking, and finds effective context length falling well short of the advertised window with the gap widening toward the edge. BABILong adds reasoning steps and finds performance dropping sharply with reasoning depth, comfortable at one hop and struggling at three. LongBench uses diverse real tasks and finds extraction from a known location degrading gracefully while synthesis across a document degrades sharply. MRCR adds multi-turn co-reference and finds accuracy dropping as the relevant history moves deeper. The summary: the retrieval half works and the synthesis half does not, so a million-token model is not a million-token reasoner.
svg.text: What the long-context benchmarks actually show
Five results, one finding: the retrieval half works, and the synthesis half degrades faster than the window suggests.
What it adds to the task

The retrieval part of long-context use works well. The synthesis and reasoning part degrades faster than the window size suggests.
A one-million-token model is not a one-million-token reasoner, which is why RAG survives: the curated subset is what the model can reason over.
